newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: FEATURE - S.Korea firms help to design better future.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - S.Korea firms help to design better future.

text.p: Could smoother curves and brighter colours on computers attract more buyers? Should men's cologne be packed in recycled cardboard for a more "rugged" look? Would dancing cartoon bears help sell electric fans?
In South Korea, product design used to be the territory of rich business conglomerates with professionals on their payroll full time to answer such questions.
But now there's a government-sponsored programme helping struggling small and medium-sized companies to better looking, and hopefully better selling, products.

Beginning in 1994, about 150 foreign designers have come to South Korea every year through a programme run by the state-backed Korea Institute of Design and Packaging (KIDP). They work with smaller firms, helping them design products that will be more competitive both at home and abroad.
Won Jin Precision Co Ltd is typical of the kind of company that benefits from the programme.
A pressed steel manufacturer of computer and facsimile casings, it is located in an industrial complex on the outskirts of Inchon City, cheek by jowl with hundreds of other small manufacturers.
With 90 employees and seven billion won in sales last year ($8.56 million), Won Jin's life-line is OEM work for South Korea's large business conglomerates. It's a small fish in a very Darwinian pond.

"Things haven't been easy for small firms," sighed Kim Heung-jae, Won Jin's director of production. "Companies like us don't have money for designers, but we still have to have good looking products to survive."
To make it possible, KIDP covers two-thirds of the salary and costs of the designer. Domestic designers also participate in the programme.
The KIDP was created in the 1970s to promote product design.

"Before, there wasn't a real need for design because people were so poor they could only buy things that were cheap and necessary," said Lee Chang-ryul, KIDP's executive managing director for international cooperation.
But times have changed. With a per capita income of around $10,000 a year, South Koreans are now sophisticated consumers with a taste for better things.
The entry of foreign products into the market is also forcing small domestic manufacturers to compete on a more global level.

Programmes like the KDIP's can mean the difference between life and death for small manufacturing firms in South Korea. While large conglomerates have thick enough financial cushions to survive, smaller firms have borne the brunt of the current economic slow-down.
"These days, most products are pretty much the same quality. So what will keep our computer cases selling better than the competitor's? The way it looks," said Won Jin's Kim.
To give Won Jin that competitve edge, New York-based British designer Stuart Harvey Lee worked on the factory floor for three weeks, creating futuristic-looking computer casings.

"The hardest part was the language barrier, but we overcame that by waving our hands a lot and drawing what we needed," he said. "I felt like I really developed a relationship with some of those guys."
"And I feel good about what I accomplished. The work I've done for them is going to be the basis of their product line for the next year."
